procedural_history.originating_court: Punjab and Haryana High Court; High Court of Delhi at New Delhi
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 28.04.2014 of the High Court of Delhi at New Delhi in W.P. (C) No. 1478 of 2012; Judgment and order of the Punjab and Haryana High Court dated 3-6-1988 made in Civil WP No. 6144 of 1987.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Punjab and Haryana High Court: Civil WP No. 6144 of 1987 resulted in a judgment and order dated 3-6-1988. Delhi High Court: W.P. (C) No. 1478 of 2012 resulted in a Judgment and Order dated 28.04.2014.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court was approached via Special Leave Petitions (SLPs). Initially, a batch of SLPs including SLP Civil No.18599/2007, questioning a decision in Social Jurists (supra), were dismissed on 1.9.2011. Sundar Lal Jain Charitable Hospital also challenged the abovesaid decision by preferring SLP (C) No.5630 of 2008 which was dismissed by reasoned order dated 01.09.2011. The present case involves Civil Appeal No. 3155 of 2007, where the Supreme Court allowed the appeals and set aside the judgment and order of the Punjab and Haryana High Court. The special leave petitions are dismissed.

reasoning.conclusion: Based on the text provided, the Supreme Court did not explain its reasoning for its decision on questions 1 and 2. However, the Court's final ruling indicates its conclusion. It found the judgment and order of the High Court to be unsustainable, quashed that decision, and allowed the appeals.

facts: Several hospitals, including Dharamshila Hospital & Research Centre and Sundar Lal Jain Charitable Hospital, filed special leave petitions.

The petitions challenged a High Court decision from a case initiated by 'Social Jurists', which directed hospitals to comply with the conditions of their land allotment, specifically the provision of free treatment to poor people.
application: The Supreme Court considered the bunch of special leave petitions, including SLP Civil No.18599/2007 and SLP (C) No.5630 of 2008.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court dismissed the special leave petitions with a reasoned, speaking order on September 1, 2011. This dismissal made the issue final, confirming the obligation of the hospitals to provide free services to the poor.

appellant_arguments: The hospital argued that there was no condition in their original agreement to provide free treatment to the economically weaker sections, and therefore, this condition was not applicable to them.

Citing the 'Divisional Manager, Aravali Golf Club & anr. v. Chander Hass & anr.' case, the appellant contended that it is not open to the Court to create a new law or an obligation that was not originally stipulated.
respondent_arguments: The Director of Health Services acted on the premise that the hospitals were obligated to provide free treatment, as evidenced by the demand to scrutinize the hospitals' accounts for compliance.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The government can enforce a pre-existing contractual and statutory liability, such as providing free medical treatment, on hospitals that obtained land under specific policies and rules for the public good, without enacting a new law, as this enforcement is not considered a new restriction on the fundamental right to practice a profession under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.
obiter: Regulations framed by the Medical Council of India also enjoin upon the medical profession to extend help.
Every act done by the Government or by its officers must, if it is to operate to the prejudice of any person, be supported by some legislative authority.
It was a self-created obligation on missionaries to do charity for which they exist while obtaining the land and Court is duty bound to enforce it.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court held that hospitals which have obtained public land at concessional rates for a charitable purpose have an inherent obligation to provide free treatment to economically weaker sections of society. This condition is not a restriction on the right to carry on a profession under Article 19(6) of the Constitution that would require a statutory law for its imposition. Instead, it is an enforceable obligation that stems from the very nature of the medical profession, the charitable purpose for which the land was granted, and the state's duty under Article 21 to ensure treatment for the poor.
legal_tests_applied: The court analyzed whether the imposition of a free treatment condition constitutes a 'restriction' under Article 19(6) of the Constitution, concluding that it is not a restriction but an inherent obligation tied to the charitable purpose of the land grant.

The court applied the principle that a judicial decision rendered in the public interest (the Social Jurists case) is applicable to all similarly situated institutions, regardless of whether they were a party to the original litigation.
The test of ‘charitable purpose’ is satisfied by the proof of any of the three conditions, namely, relief of the poor, education, or medical relief.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the appellant's primary argument that the condition for free treatment could only be imposed by a statutory law, holding: 'In our considered opinion the High Court has erred in law in holding that such stipulation could have been imposed only by a statutory law. In our considered opinion, it is not a restriction on the right to carry on medical profession...'

The court dismissed the appellant's contention that the decision in the 'Social Jurists' case was not applicable to them, stating: 'The decision rendered in Social Jurists case would be applicable to similarly situated institutions having been rendered in the public interest institution and affirmed by this Court by a reasoned order.'

The court found that the obligation for free treatment was intrinsically linked to the benefit the hospitals received, reasoning that 'in lieu of holding land of Government at concessional rate and enjoying huge occupancy benefits... the hospitals can be asked to impart free treatment as envisaged in the Government order.'
why_respondent_won: The court affirmed the government's power to impose the condition, stating that 'when the Government land had been obtained for charitable purpose of running the hospital, the Government is within its right to impose such an obligation.'

The court established that the obligation is rooted in the very definition of the activity, finding that 'when the State land is being held which is for the public good with no profit motive, such land is held for the charitable purpose of public good. The charitable purpose would include... the aforesaid obligation of free treatment to the persons of economically weaker strata of the society.'

The court found a constitutional basis for the obligation, holding that 'members of the medical profession owe a constitutional duty to treat the have-nots. They cannot refuse to treat a person who is in dire need of treatment... merely on the ground that he is not in a position to afford the fee...'
policy_considerations: The poor cannot be deprived of the treatment by the best physician due to his economic disability in case he requires it. It is the obligation on the medical professionals, hospitals, the State and all concerned to ensure that such person is given treatment and not deprived of the same due to poverty.

On the making of a doctor, the State spends and invests a huge amount of public money and it is the corresponding obligation to serve the needy and the treatment cannot be refused on the ground of financial inability of the patient to bear it.

The benefits of various welfare schemes hardly reach to them in spite of efforts made, economic disparity is writ large and persists. They cannot afford such treatment and thus in lieu of holding land of Government at concessional rate and enjoying huge occupancy benefits... the hospitals can be asked to impart free treatment...
The moment it is permitted, the medical profession would become purely a commercial activity, it is not supposed to be so due to its nobleness.
